writing.exampleCaption: Classification checklist for Monotonic Decreasing Stack
writing.explanation:
A problem is a good match for Monotonic Decreasing Stack when it asks for stock span, next greater, visibility. Here the concrete task is: Return the number of consecutive earlier days with price less than or equal to today. The visible input `[100,80,60,70,60,75,85]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Look for nested structure, next-greater relationships, or ordered processing. A plain scan is enough when no unresolved state must be retained. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Pop smaller candidates so unresolved values remain in decreasing order. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A stack remembers unfinished work in last-in-first-out order; a queue processes work in first-in-first-out order. Say what each stored item still needs. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n) time · O(n) space; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `1,1,1,2,1,4,6` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Check empty containers, one item, repeated equal values, and the work left in the structure after the input ends. Vec works as a stack; VecDeque supplies efficient operations at both ends. Avoid removing from the front of a Vec in a long loop. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
